source.title: Disentangling the Causes of Plasticity Loss in Neural Networks
source.authors: Clare Lyle; Ze-Yu Zheng; Khimya Khetarpal; H. V. Hasselt; Razvan Pascanu; James Martens; Will Dabney

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports training accuracy and learning behavior while networks train on sequentially changing classification tasks, and compares depth and width. These results bear on training plasticity but do not reproduce the fixed-task recipes in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study measures training accuracy on sequential classification tasks, including random-label memorization. Rows below cover explicit text results and figure-only outcomes; cited prior work is not included.
record.test_reason: The study directly reports that batch normalization improves convergence rates within sequential classification tasks, bearing on V6 in a new, nonstationary setting. Most extracted rows instead measure continued adaptation from previously trained parameters, outside V1's random-initialization condition. The depth sweep does not establish V3's batch-normalized plain-versus-residual comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate, but needs qualification: independent mechanisms account for many observed plasticity failures, and combining interventions helps. Layer normalization plus L2 regularization is effective in supervised nonstationary tasks; L2 and batch normalization can interfere with deep RL, where the authors emphasize layer normalization and scale-invariant output losses. L2 regularization can also slow single-task convergence. Width helps in the architecture sweep, while depth helps permuted-class tasks and hurts random-label tasks without additional tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies ongoing adaptation under nonstationarity, using Adam in the continual supervised-learning setup and evaluating normalization and regularization interventions; it does not reproduce the fixed-task training recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Label-reset fraction, task type, network depth and width, normalization, L2 penalty, and architecture affect the reported training behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Abrupt label changes cause greater loss of subsequent training accuracy than gradual changes; layer normalization with L2 regularization helps preserve adaptation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Previously trained networks can lose plasticity under nonstationarity, with severity depending on task-change magnitude and mitigation.

fits_no_version.finding: Greater width improves sequential-task performance; greater depth hurts random-label performance without depth-specific tuning but improves permuted-class performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture affects robustness to nonstationarity differently across task types.

fits_no_version.finding: Large pretraining target means impair subsequent regression learning, and plasticity loss accompanies feature and empirical-NTK degeneracies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training history can impair later optimization through target-mean effects, preactivation shifts, and parameter growth.

record.problems: The depth sweep used a learning rate tuned for depth 4 and no additional depth-specific hyperparameter sweeps. Several plotted outcomes are figure-only in the supplied text, and the study focuses on sequential nonstationarity rather than the fixed-task claim.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were required beyond the selected results; several figures contain curves for other task modes, activation functions, and interventions, but the text does not assign precise values to each plotted condition.

untested.parts: The near-zero training classification error claim for sufficiently large CNNs trained from random initialization on fixed CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 tasks. First-task difficulty and learning-rate selection do not establish the claimed error levels.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and adding one or two student neurons.
Depth degradation in batch-normalized plain CNNs versus matched identity-shortcut networks, longer-training controls, deep tanh initialization, and Fixup.
Activation-matched signal-preserving initialization comparisons, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth. The positive-weight toy experiment does not establish these comparisons.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, catapult recovery, and sustained edge-of-stability dynamics. Parameter-norm and Hessian correlations do not test these predictions.
Tolerance of higher learning rates, the original stationary benchmark recipes, and Fixup's speed and stability without normalization.

missing.what: Batch-normalization versus unnormalized training comparisons for within-task convergence. Section 4.1 explicitly reports convergence benefits, but no extracted row records them. Preserve architecture and normalization combinations and do not infer numerical speedups from the supplied figure text.
missing.locator: Section 4.1, 'Unbounded norm growth' and 'Preactivation statistics'; Figure 4

record.verdict_notes: No numerical curve values were reconstructed. States marked cannot_determine reflect inability to establish a claim version, not uncertainty about the reported direction of plasticity changes. R7 and R8 should be consolidated with R6 and R5.

versions.untested_parts: Fixed-task training from random initialization on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100; comparisons of SGD versus Adam; corrupted or random labels without sequential relabeling; smaller models and early-stopping recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and spurious minima.
Batch-normalized plain CNNs versus the same networks with identity residual shortcuts; ImageNet; whether longer training remedies the depth effect.
Activation-matched initializations, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and 10,000-layer plain CNN training.
Learning rates above stability thresholds, curvature dynamics, and divergence.
Batch normalization's speed and learning-rate effects and Fixup training without normalization.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Continued training on CIFAR-10 with a fraction of randomly assigned labels re-randomized at each task change.

conditions.value: ReLU, GeLU, and Leaky ReLU (negative slope 0.01)

rows.measure: Training accuracy over sequential random-label tasks
rows.value: Resetting only 1% of labels minimally interferes with performance.
rows.note: The text reports this qualitative result across the stated activation functions; the precise values appear only in the figure.
rows.check: Minimal interference from 1% relabeling measures retained plasticity, not near-zero training error from random initialization. Appendix B.1 supplies the default CNN architecture omitted from the row.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Continued training on CIFAR-10 with a fraction of randomly assigned labels re-randomized at each task change.

conditions.value: ReLU, GeLU, and Leaky ReLU (negative slope 0.01)

rows.measure: Training accuracy over sequential random-label tasks
rows.value: Increasing this fraction to 10% rapidly accelerates the decline.
rows.note: The paper describes a decline in performance as the fraction of labels reset increases; this is sequential training, not a fixed-task run.
rows.check: Declining accuracy after sequential relabeling does not test V1's random-initialization condition or quantify proximity to zero training error.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Training with layer normalization before each nonlinearity and an L2 penalty on sequential CIFAR-10 tasks.
rows.note: The text says accuracy tends to improve over time for the evaluated architectures and modes, but does not assign the plotted values to this specific condition.
rows.check: This MLP's continued adaptation with layer normalization and L2 regularization does not measure V1's convolutional-network claim. The supplied figure text cannot establish this condition's accuracy.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.size_stated: depth 4, 32 channels, fully connected hidden layer width 256 by default
rows.operation_detail: Compared network widths in sequential random-label memorization and permuted-class tasks.
rows.note: The authors state that increasing width gives consistent improvements; plotted numeric values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Relative accuracy improvements from width during sequential adaptation do not establish near-zero error from random initialization. Width alone also does not test V2's teacher-student local-minimum claim.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared network depths in sequential random-label and permuted-class tasks.

conditions.value: tuned for depth 4 network; no additional depth-specific hyperparameter sweeps

rows.note: The authors say increased depth without additional hyperparameter tuning reduces performance and accelerates plasticity loss in the random-label task.
rows.check: An MLP depth sweep does not test V1's CNN claim or V3's batch-normalized CNN comparison. Reduced accuracy is an observed adverse depth effect, not evidence reversing either version.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared network depths in sequential random-label and permuted-class tasks.

conditions.value: tuned for depth 4 network; no additional depth-specific hyperparameter sweeps

rows.note: The authors say increased depth without additional hyperparameter tuning reduces performance and accelerates plasticity loss in the random-label task.
rows.check: The reported sequential depth disadvantage does not establish whether sufficiently large CNNs reach near-zero error from random initialization. Greater difficulty on the first task is also reported, but without readable error levels or an established capacity criterion. Duplicated in R7.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared depth in sequential image-classification tasks.

conditions.value: tuned for depth 4 network; no additional depth-specific hyperparameter sweeps

rows.note: The authors report reduced performance and faster plasticity loss with greater depth in this setting; the paper's normalization and residual-shortcut comparison does not match V3's specified setup.
rows.check: Duplicates R6. The sweep does not establish batch-normalized plain CNNs or a matched residual comparison. Its adverse depth effect points in V3's stated direction, so 'reversed' is incorrect even as a directional description.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared depth in sequential image-classification tasks.

conditions.value: tuned for depth 4 network; no additional depth-specific hyperparameter sweeps

rows.note: The authors report reduced performance and faster plasticity loss with greater depth in this setting; the paper does not test the specified batch-normalized CNN and identity-shortcut comparison.
rows.check: Duplicates R5. MLPs are outside V3's specified convolutional architectures; no matched identity-shortcut comparison is provided.

relationships.condition: Batch-normalized networks on the study's sequential supervised classification tasks
relationships.reason: Section 4.1 explicitly reports improved within-task convergence rates from preactivation normalization, including batch normalization; this verdict rests on text because the relevant comparison is missing from the rows.
relationships.display_finding: Preactivation normalization, including batch normalization, improved within-task convergence rates.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
